look_here_first: Start at the base of the plant. Texas spiderwort is low, many-stemmed and bushy at ground level, with clearly hairy vegetative shoots; toward the inflorescence the hairs become strongly glandular. That compact, fuzzy architecture separates it quickly from the taller giant and prairie spiderworts.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: compact ascending/spreading shoots, under 20 cm in the Williamson treatment

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: leaf blades pilose with hairs reaching several millimeters

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: inflorescence and pedicels conspicuously stalked-glandular hairy

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: terminal condensed cyme, usually 1–2 flowers open per day

lookalikes.differences: T. gigantea is taller and more robust with lower stems nearly glabrous. T. occidentalis is taller and grassier, with narrow leaves and especially conspicuous glandular stem/peduncle hairs. T. humilis stays low and bushy with hairy blades.
